(p-643)Surah "al-Balad" (The City)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿I swear by this city﴾. He, glory be to Him, swears by the Sacred City (al-Balad al-Haram) and by what follows it, that man was created immersed in toil and hardship. He interposed, between the oath and the thing sworn to, the words:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 90, verse 2:

﴿And you are a lawful resident in this city.﴾ That is: and part of the hardship is that someone like you, despite the greatness of your sanctity, is made lawful (yustahall) in this city, meaning Makkah, just as game is made lawful outside the sacred precinct (haram). From Shurahbil: "They consider it forbidden to kill game therein, yet they consider it lawful to expel you and to kill you." In this there is reassurance (tathbit) for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and an urging to bear what he was enduring from the people of Makkah, and an expression of wonder at their state in their enmity towards him. Or: He consoled the Messenger of Allah by swearing by his city, since a human being is never free of enduring hardships. An objection is raised: He promised him the conquest of Makkah, as a completion of the consolation and relief for him, so He said: "﴿And you are a lawful resident in this city﴾", meaning: and you will be a lawful resident in it in the future, doing in it whatever you wish, of killing and capturing. That is because Allah (Exalted) granted him the conquest of Makkah and made it lawful for him, and it was not conquered for anyone before him nor made lawful for anyone else. So he made lawful what he willed and forbade what he willed. He killed Ibn Khatal while he was clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah, and Miqyas ibn Subabah, and others. And he forbade the house of (p-644) Abu Sufyan. The parallel to His saying "And you are a lawful resident" in the future tense is His saying: ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed they will die﴾ [al-Zumar: 30]. And sufficient as evidence that it refers to the future is that the surah is Makkan by consensus, and where was the Hijrah at the time of its revelation?! So what of the conquest?!

**﴿And by the begetter and what he begot﴾**: they are Adam and his offspring; or every begetter and his offspring; or Abraham and his offspring. And "mā" (what) is in the sense of "man" (who), or in the sense of "alladhī" (which/that who).

﴿Indeed, We created man﴾, the answer to the oath,

﴿in toil﴾, in hardship; he endures the calamities of this world and the severities of the Hereafter. And from Dhu'l-Nun (Dhu'n-Nun): "He has never ceased to be bound by the rope of decree, being called to obey and to refrain."

The pronoun in ﴿Does he think that no one has power over him?﴾ refers to some of the chiefs (ṣanādīd) of Quraysh, those with whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to struggle greatly. Then it was said: he is Abū al-Ashadd, and it was said: al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra. The meaning is: Does this powerful chief among his people, who oppresses the believers, think that there will be no Resurrection and that no one will be able to take revenge on him? Then He mentioned what he would say on that Day, and that he...

﴿He says: I have squandered wealth in abundance﴾. I.e., much, the plural of "lubdah" (a mass), which is what has become matted (talabbada), meaning it has accumulated and gathered together. He means the great quantity of what he spent on what the people of the Jahiliyyah (the time of ignorance before Islam) used to call noble deeds (makarim) and lofty acts (ma'ali).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 90, verse 7:

﴿Does he think that no one sees him?﴾ — when he spent what he spent out of showing off and boasting. The meaning is that Allah (Exalted) was seeing him, and was watching over him. Then He mentioned His blessings upon him, saying:

Translation of the passage:

﴿Did We not make for him two eyes?﴾ with which he sees visible things?!

﴿And a tongue﴾, by which he expresses what is in his heart,

﴿and two lips﴾, with which he covers his mouth, and by which he is aided in speech, eating, drinking, and blowing.
﴿And We guided him to the two highways﴾, the paths of good and evil, which lead to the Garden and the Fire. And it is said: the two breasts.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 90, verses 11–17:

﴿But he has not attempted the steep path.﴾ ﴿And what can make you know what the steep path is?﴾ ﴿It is freeing a slave;﴾ ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger,﴾ ﴿an orphan of near relationship,﴾ ﴿or a needy person in misery;﴾ ﴿and then being among those who believed.﴾ Meaning: he did not give thanks for those favours and blessings through righteous deeds, such as freeing slaves or feeding orphans and the needy, and then through faith, which is the root of every act of obedience and the foundation of all good. Rather, he ungratefully rejected the blessings and disbelieved in the Bestower. The meaning is that spending in this manner is pleasing and beneficial in the sight of God, not that one wastes his wealth in heaps out of showing off and boasting.

"Lā" (the negative particle) is rarely used with the past tense except when repeated. In the more eloquent speech it is not repeated, because when the attempt at the steep path was explained by three things, it was as if "lā" had been repeated three times. Its implied sense is: "He did not free a slave, nor feed a needy person, nor believe."

"Iqtiḥām" means entering and passing through something with force and hardship, and "al-quḥmah" means severity. He made righteous deeds a steep path and doing them an attempt at it, because of the hardship and the struggle against the self that they involve. Al-Ḥasan said: "By God, it is a steep path: a person's striving against his own self and his desire, or against his enemy, Satan."

His saying "What is the steep path?" means: what is the attempt at it? The meaning is that you do not know the full difficulty of it for the self, nor the full reward of it with God.

"Fakk al-raqabah" means freeing the neck from slavery, or assisting in the ransom contract (kitābah, the agreement by which a slave buys his freedom). The reading "faka raqabatan aw aṭ'ama" is that of Makkī, Abū ʿAmr and ʿAlī, in apposition (ibdāl, substitution) to "iqtaḥama al-ʿaqabah". His saying "wa-mā adrāka mā al-ʿaqabah" is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ, interjection). Others read "fakku raqabatin aw iṭʿāmun" as "iqtiḥāmuhā fakku raqabatin aw iṭʿāmun" (its attempt is freeing a slave or feeding).

"Al-masghabah" means hunger, "al-maqrabah" means kinship, and "al-matrabah" means poverty. They are of the pattern "mafʿalah" from "sagha" (he became hungry), and "qaruba" in lineage, as one says: "Fulān dhū qarābatī" and "dhū maqrabatī" (he is my relative). "Taraba" means he became destitute, and its meaning is that he cleaved to the dust, so that his dwelling is the rubbish heaps. He described the day as "dhī masghabah" in the manner of their saying "hammun nāṣib" (a wearying worry), meaning "dhū naṣab" (possessing weariness).

The meaning of "thumma kāna min alladhīna āmanū" is that he persevered in faith. It has also been said that "thumma" here means "wa" (and). It has also been said that "thumma" was used to indicate the remoteness of faith and its distance in rank and excellence from emancipation and charity, not in time, since faith is what precedes all else, and no righteous deed is established without it.

﴿And they enjoined one another to patience,﴾ in refraining from sins, and in acts of obedience and the trials with which the believer is tested.

﴿And they enjoined one another to compassion,﴾ showing mercy to one another among themselves.

Others read "fakku raqabatin aw iṭʿāmun" as "iqtiḥāmuhā fakku raqabatin aw iṭʿāmun" (its attempt is freeing a slave or feeding).

"Al-masghabah" means hunger, "al-maqrabah" means kinship, and "al-matrabah" means poverty. They are of the pattern "mafʿalah" from "sagha" (he became hungry), and "qaruba" in lineage, as one says: "Fulān dhū qarābatī" and "dhū maqrabatī" (he is my relative). "Taraba" means he became destitute, and its meaning is that he cleaved to the dust, so that his dwelling is the rubbish heaps. He described the day as "dhī masghabah" in the manner of their saying "hammun nāṣib" (a wearying worry), meaning "dhū naṣab" (possessing weariness).

The meaning of "thumma kāna min alladhīna āmanū" is that he persevered in faith. It has also been said that "thumma" here means "wa" (and). It has also been said that "thumma" was used to indicate the remoteness of faith and its distance in rank and excellence from emancipation and charity, not in time, since faith is what precedes all else, and no righteous deed is established without it.

﴿And they enjoined one another to patience,﴾ in refraining from sins, and in acts of obedience and the trials with which the believer is tested.

﴿And they enjoined one another to compassion,﴾ showing mercy to one another among themselves.
(p-646) ﴿Those are the companions of the right hand﴾, i.e., those who are described by these attributes are among the companions of the right (aṣḥāb al-yamīn).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 90, verse 19:

﴿And those who disbelieve in Our signs﴾, i.e., in the Qur'an, or in Our proofs,

﴿they are the companions of the left hand (al-mash'ama)﴾, the companions of the left side. Al-maymana and al-mash'ama mean the right and the left, or the blessing and the ill omen. That is, the people of the right (al-mayamin) are those who are fortunate for themselves, and the people of the left (al-mashá'im) are those who are unfortunate for themselves.

﴿عَلَيْهِمْ نَارٌ مُّؤْصَدَةٌ﴾ [Upon them will be a fire closed in]. With the hamza (مُؤْصَدَةٌ), as read by Abu 'Amr, Hamza and Hafs. Meaning: مُطْبِقَةٌ (muṭbiqah), closed over and sealed, from "أَوْصَدْتُ البابَ" (awṣadtu al-bāb, "I closed the door") and "آصَدْتُهُ" (āṣadtuhu), when I shut it tight and locked it.
